q: In which Corstorphine park did Hibs win their first Edinburgh Cup by beating Hearts in 1879?
info: Union Park! Hibernian beat Hearts 2–0 in the Edinburgh Cup final replay in 1879. Hearts had won the 1878 final.

q: From which local green space might you spot zebras?
info: Corstorphine Hill overlooks Edinburgh Zoo, so a zebra sighting is possible from the hill.

q: Where did Olympic champion Eric Liddell later run a 440-yard race?
info: Union Park hosted a race involving Eric Liddell, the runner celebrated in Chariots of Fire.

q: Which local hill has signs of human activity from roughly 5,000 years ago?
info: Corstorphine Hill has ancient cup-and-ring markings showing very early human activity.

q: Which park did author Irvine Welsh visit on breaks from his nearby workplace?
info: St Margaret’s Park is linked to Irvine Welsh, who worked nearby at Ladywell House.

q: What famous aerobatic display team is shown flying over Corstorphine in this photo?
a: The Battle of Britain Memorial Flight
info: The Red Arrows are the Royal Air Force aerobatic team, famous for their precision flying and smoke trails.

q: Which park is overlooked by a church designed by architect Sir Basil Spence?
info: Clermiston Park is overlooked by St Andrew’s Church, designed by Sir Basil Spence.

q: Which local park was used for annual Hearts supporters’ outings?
info: St Margaret’s Park hosted annual Hearts supporters’ outings. The original Corstorphine Fair quiz also links these visits with the longer permitted opening hours of local pubs.

q: Which local place name comes from Gaelic for “brow of the ridge”?
info: Drum Brae comes from the Gaelic Druim Bràigh.

q: Which park was created in 1961?
info: Drum Brae Park is the youngest of the parks featured in this quiz.

q: Which park has Drum Brae Library opposite it?
info: Clermiston Park has Drum Brae Library opposite it.

q: Which hill is one of Corstorphine’s best-known places for views over the city and beyond?
info: Corstorphine Hill is famous for its views, woodland walks and links to local history and wildlife.

q: What is the earliest recorded spelling of Corstorphine, appearing in a charter from 1128?
info: Crostorfin (also recorded as Crostorfyn) appears in early records associated with David I and Holyrood Abbey.

q: Which medieval family acquired Corstorphine lands during the 1370s?
info: Sir Adam Forrester bought Corstorphine lands in the 1370s. His family later became closely associated with the castle and church.

q: In which year was Corstorphine incorporated into Edinburgh?
info: Corstorphine became part of Edinburgh in 1920.

q: Which building survives from the old Corstorphine Castle estate?
info: The 16th-century Corstorphine Dovecot, or Doocot, survives from the castle estate.

q: Roughly how many nesting boxes are inside Corstorphine Dovecot?
info: The dovecot has about 1,060 nesting boxes for pigeons.

q: What kind of famous tree stood by the Corstorphine Dovecot until 1998?
info: The Sycamore of Corstorphine was lost during the Boxing Day storms in 1998.

q: Which nobleman was killed in 1679 in the story associated with Christian Nimmo and the Corstorphine sycamore?
info: James Forrester, 2nd Lord Forrester, was murdered in 1679. Christian Nimmo was convicted of his murder.

q: To which saint is Corstorphine Old Parish Church dedicated?
info: The church is dedicated to St John the Baptist and developed from the medieval collegiate church.

q: What unusual ground plan is associated with Corstorphine Old Parish Church?
info: Its medieval layout is often described as a Jerusalem Cross or cruciform plan.

q: What was the celebrated old local delicacy called “Corstorphine Cream”?
info: It was a thickened soured-milk delicacy, traditionally made by adding warm milk to buttermilk.

q: What is the nickname of the tiny building on St John’s Road measuring only about 40 inches wide?
info: The Wee Shop has been used for several different small businesses over the years.

q: Which park was donated by Christopher Douglas Brown and opened in 1915?
info: St Margaret’s Park was gifted to the community and opened in 1915.

q: What is the name of the historic building in St Margaret’s Park housing the Heritage Centre?
info: The Dower House, also known as Gibson’s Lodge, is home to the Corstorphine Heritage Centre.

q: Which famous writer is commemorated by the tower on Corstorphine Hill?
info: The tower commemorates Sir Walter Scott and was built for the centenary of his birth.

q: What is another local name for Corstorphine Hill Tower?
info: The landmark is commonly called Clermiston Tower, and is also known as Scott Tower.

q: In which year did Edinburgh Zoo first open?
info: Edinburgh Zoo opened in 1913 on the slopes of Corstorphine Hill.

q: What was the name of the bear that served with Polish soldiers and later lived at Edinburgh Zoo?
info: Wojtek, a Syrian brown bear, travelled with the Polish II Corps during the Second World War and later lived at Edinburgh Zoo.

q: What military rank did Edinburgh Zoo’s king penguin Sir Nils Olav III reach in 2023?
info: Sir Nils Olav III became a Major General in the Norwegian King’s Guard in 2023, after having been a Brigadier since 2016.

q: Which pioneering suffragist and University of Edinburgh science graduate grew up in Corstorphine?
info: Chrystal Macmillan was a pioneering suffragist, lawyer and the first woman to graduate in science from the University of Edinburgh.

q: In which Robert Louis Stevenson novel does David Balfour pass through Corstorphine?
info: David Balfour travels through the area in Kidnapped, first published in 1886.

q: Which two lochs once lay on either side of old Corstorphine?
info: Corstorphine Loch lay to the east and Gogar Loch to the west. The low-lying ground was once much wetter than it is today.

q: By which decade had Corstorphine’s old lochs been completely drained?
info: Drainage began in the 1660s and was completed by about 1837. Much of the old loch area became meadowland.

q: What is the name of the old drainage watercourse associated with Corstorphine’s lochs?
info: The Stank Burn connected the wet ground around Corstorphine and was altered during centuries of drainage work.

q: What sort of mineral water made Corstorphine’s Physic Well a fashionable 18th-century attraction?
info: The Physic Well was known for its sulphurous mineral water. In 1749 a stagecoach began bringing visitors from Edinburgh.

q: Where can you find surviving restored stonework associated with Corstorphine’s Physic Well?
a: At the bottom of Dunsmuir Court
info: The stone edging near Dunsmuir Court was restored in 1972–73 after being buried. The original well was nearby.

q: Which historic well name is remembered in Corstorphine street names?
info: Ladywell survives in local street names. Historical accounts also associate a Well of Our Lady with the site of the later Physic Well.

q: In what year did the North British Railway open the Corstorphine branch line and terminus?
info: The terminus opened on 1 February 1902, connecting Corstorphine with Edinburgh by rail.

q: How long did the journey from Corstorphine station to Edinburgh Waverley take?
info: Just 11 minutes! That was the advertised journey time on the former Corstorphine branch.

q: In what year did Corstorphine railway station close to passenger services?
info: Passenger services ended on 1 January 1968, following the last trains in December 1967. Freight ceased in February.

q: What now occupies the former site of Corstorphine railway station?
info: The old station site was redeveloped for housing at The Paddockholm, near Station Road.

q: Which St John’s Road pub is named after a ghost linked to Christian Nimmo and the 1679 murder of Lord Forrester?
info: The White Lady takes its name from a local ghost story. Christian Nimmo was convicted of killing Lord Forrester in 1679, and folklore associates her ghost with a sycamore tree near the dovecot.

q: Which old St John’s Road inn once welcomed horse-drawn buses and was later replaced by The Torfin?
info: The Oak Inn, also called The Oak, was one of the old coaching stops on St John’s Road. The Torfin later took its place.

q: What is the traditional nickname of the Corstorphine Inn, and which game facility did it lose?
info: Locals call the Corstorphine Inn “the Corrie”. It once had a skittle alley, which was removed during alterations.

q: Which inn once stood near the High Street and Saughton Road corner called Irish Corner?
info: The Black Bull Inn gave the corner its landmark. The area was called Irish Corner because Irish workers lived nearby, including people who came for canal and railway construction.

q: Why was the Mansion House near Corstorphine Primary School originally built around 1750?
a: As lodging for visitors taking the Physic Well waters
info: The Mansion House was a kind of spa lodging house for visitors who came to drink the water from the Physic Well. It was demolished in 1952 as the school expanded.

q: What traditional Scots name was used for Manse Road, the narrow lane leading towards St Ninian’s?
info: It was known as “the Slap” or “Barney’s Slap”. Locals spoke of going “down the Loan” and “up the Slap”.

q: What formed the old Cross of Corstorphine, recalled in the name Cross Cottages?
a: Five elm trees arranged as a square with one in the middle
Four standing stones in a straight line
A stone cross beside three yew trees
Six oak trees around a village pump
info: The Cross of Corstorphine was a group of five elm trees: one at each corner of a square and a fifth in the centre. Nearby houses were called Cross Cottages.

q: According to local accounts, who gave Traquair Park its name?
info: Local accounts attribute the name to Maud Traquair, mother of John and W. Traquair Dickson, whose family was associated with Corstorphine House.

q: Which Corstorphine Hill viewpoint, mentioned in Kidnapped, gave its name to a nearby road?
info: Rest and Be Thankful is a traditional stopping point on Corstorphine Hill. Robert Louis Stevenson mentions it in Kidnapped as David Balfour and Alan Breck near Edinburgh.

q: What surprising clothing trade once operated in Corstorphine’s tiny Wee Shop on St John’s Road?
info: The Wee Shop’s occupants have reportedly included a corsetry maker or staymaker — remarkable given how tiny the premises are.

q: In what year was Corstorphine Primary School first founded near its current site?
info: The first Lord Forrester established Corstorphine School in 1646. Later school buildings followed, including one built in 1848.

q: Which two symbols feature on Corstorphine Primary School’s badge?
a: A hunting horn and a lamp
info: The school badge combines a Forrester hunting horn with a lamp. The lamp recalls the old light that guided travellers across marshy ground.

q: Which Catholic boys’ school operated at Beechwood House on Corstorphine Road from 1953 to 1978?
info: Scotus Academy opened at Beechwood House in 1953. It was run by the Christian Brothers.

q: What was St Ninian’s Church on St John’s Road originally called when it opened in 1844?
info: It began as Corstorphine Free Church after the 1843 Disruption. It adopted the name St Ninian’s in 1929.

q: The Victorian gas lamps in St Ninian’s Church originally came from which Edinburgh meeting place?
info: The church’s first minister, the Rev Dr George Burns, obtained its gasoliers from the hall at Tanfield, where the Free Church’s first General Assembly met in 1843.

q: What wood was used for the large cross installed in St Ninian’s Church during its 1953 refurbishment?
info: The cross was made from sycamore to connect the church with Corstorphine’s historic sycamore tree.

q: On which local road does the Corstorphine War Memorial stand?
info: The Corstorphine War Memorial stands on Kirk Loan, beside Corstorphine Old Parish Church.

q: Which heraldic emblem appears on the Corstorphine War Memorial’s shield?
info: The three hunting horns are associated with the arms of the Forrester family of Corstorphine.

q: In what year was Corstorphine Curling Club founded?
info: Corstorphine Curling Club dates from 1829, when outdoor ice was central to the sport.

q: In what year was Corstorphine Bowling Club formed?
info: Corstorphine Bowling Club was founded on 27 July 1891. Its first green was in the grounds of Dunsmuir.

q: What Roman-era objects have been found on Corstorphine Hill?
info: Fragments of Roman pottery are among the archaeological finds recorded on Corstorphine Hill. They do not by themselves prove there was a Roman fort on the hill.

q: An enclosure at Broomhall has been suggested as what kind of Roman site?
info: The Broomhall enclosure has been interpreted as a possible Roman fort, but its Roman date and function remain unconfirmed.

q: Near which place was a Roman milestone found that helps reveal Roman roads west of Edinburgh?
info: The Ingliston milestone names the First Cohort of Cugerni and dates to the Antonine period, around AD 140–144.

q: Why did visitors travel to Corstorphine in the 1700s?
a: To take the mineral waters at the Physic Well
To see the first Edinburgh Zoo penguins
To ride a railway into the city
info: Corstorphine’s sulphurous Physic Well became a fashionable spa attraction in the eighteenth century, with visitors travelling out from Edinburgh.

q: Why were annual Hearts supporters’ outings to St Margaret’s Park associated with Corstorphine pubs?
a: Local drinking rules could allow longer opening for qualifying travellers
The park had its own football stadium
Every visitor received a free match ticket
The pubs were owned by Hearts
info: The original Corstorphine Fair quiz links the annual outings with the rules that allowed qualifying travellers to be served in hotel premises on Sundays.

q: In which year did Hibernian first win the Edinburgh Cup, defeating Hearts in a replay at Corstorphine?
info: Hibernian won the 1879 Edinburgh Cup after defeating Hearts 2–0 in the final replay. Hearts had taken the title in 1878.
